content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors provide a method for normalizing flows on SO(3) by adapting a method on spheres from previous work. They define a coupling layer on rotation matrices and an affine transformation on quaternions, which are repeated to deform SO(3) with an invertible transformation. content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- There are a larger number of interesting tricks in this work that enable the generalization of the previous method on spheres to SO(3).
- The results on synthetic benchmarks show that the method works better than alternatives and is able to successfully fit multimodal distributions on SO(3)

Weaknesses:
- The work is lacking insight into why the individual operations (Möbius Coupling, Affine Transformations) are reasonable choices for what they are supposed to achieve.
- The work is very incremental to previous work [1], partially follows the same structure and uses similar explanations. Meanwhile, the previous work does a better job in explaining the concepts on theoretic and intuitive level.

content.title: Author Response(1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback. Our immediate response to some comments is below:

> The work is very incremental to previous work [1], partially follows the same structure and uses similar explanations. Meanwhile, the previous work does a better job in explaining the concepts on theoretic and intuitive level.

We disagree with the idea and stress the novelty of our mobius coupling layer and affine transformation. The design of Mobius coupling layers which utilized the geometry features of rotation matrix, that the 3 columns are orthonormal to each other is untrivial and can be interpreted more elegantly as a bundle isomorphism. It uses the fiber bundle with projection $\pi:SO(3)\rightarrow SO(2)$ and fiber $S^1 = SO(2)$ . Choosing the conditioning dimension $i=1,2,3$  defines one such projection, for each base space point $c_1$ , there is a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(c_1) \rightarrow \pi^{-1}(c_1)$ over its fiber, which together forms a base-space preserving bundle isomorphism. Our mobius coupling layers may help generalization to other fiber bundles.

The affine transformation which greatly accelerates learning and improves performance is crucial to hard tasks like conditional rotation regress and will be explained in detail later.

> The authors claim that the model can be conditioned but have no experiment validating that.

We present conditional rotation regression tasks in section 4.2. We experiment on SYMSOL dataset introduced by Murphy et al. (2021). SYMSOL I contained images with solids with a high order of symmetry, e.g., cube, cone, and SYMSOL II include solids with a small marker to break the regular symmetries. We followed the same experiment setting Murphy et al. (2021), and our results both in log-likelihood and in spread metric outperform all the baselines significantly.

Some illustrations of images from SYMSOL, our learned distributions, and ground pose will be updated in our paper soon.

> It is not that hard to parameterize a rotation matrix. This can be done by parameterizing a unit quaternion and converting it to a rotation matrix quite effectively. Why is that not done instead of mapping the rotation matrix to a quaternion and back?

Affine flow on quaternion performs 2 functions: a rotation operation and a scaling operation. The rotation operation not only makes it easier to learn a global rotation but also serves as a generalization of permutation in our mobius coupling layers. The scaling operation can quickly concentrate distributions and can accelerate the learning speed as shown by the ablation study on SYMSOL. It's really surprising that 2 operations can be done in a single affine flow layer, and the mathematical expression is elegant and simple. That s why we choose to implement quaternion affine flows rather than separately implement rotation on a rotation matrix.

> The work is lacking insight into why the individual operations (Möbius Coupling, Affine Transformations) are reasonable choices for what they are supposed to achieve.

Ablation study on synthetic data showed that Mobius transformation is of crucial importance for modeling the cube-like multimodal distributions, and affine transformation generally improved the overall performance. Our further ablation study on SYMSOL I showed that Mobius Coupling layers are the basic part of our flows, without which will reduce the performance dramatically when the task is hard, and Affine flows improve the performance and accelerate the learning with the ability to quickly concentrate the density and learn a global rotation.

It shows that without mobius coupling layers, the affine flows is not sufficient to learn the complex multi-modal distribution. With long enough iterations(about 7 days), flows with mobius coupling layers can reach very high performance, and the affine flows greatly accelerate the process(about 1-2 days). For the 2 functions of affine transformation, the scaling operation is more important as it helps to quickly concentrate density and make accurate predictions. The detailed result will be updated in our paper soon. 

> The method is only evaluated on toy benchmarks, there seem to be no real application the authors can evaluate on.

We present applications of conditional rotation regression tasks in which our results outperform SOTA and entropy estimation in which our results show that even with very few samples(~10), the Monte-Carlo estimation can be accurate where as ipdf needs (~1000) samples to reach the same stage.

content.title: Author Response(2/2)
content.comment:
> Previous work [1] presents a method for general $S^d$. Why can this method not directly be applied to SO(3) using the unit quaternion representation (using the symmetry enforcement that is used anyway)? It seems that it would be much easier than the construction on rotation matrices presented here.

Work by Rezende et.al. presents 2 methods for general $S^d$: a recursive construction that used cylindrical coordinates, and a construction based on the exponential map.

Take S^3 for specific, the recursive construction follows a map:

$$
S^3 \rightarrow S^2 \times [-1, 1] \rightarrow S^1 \times [-1,1] \times [-1, 1]\rightarrow S^1 \times [-1,1] \times [-1, 1] \rightarrow S^2 \times [-1, 1] \rightarrow S^3
$$

The sphere $S^D$ is recursively transformed into a "cylinder", and applied an autoregressive flow on $S^1 \times [-1, 1]^{D-1}$, and transformed back to $S^D$. However, as the topology of "cylinder" and sphere $S^D$ differ, these maps between $S^D$ and $S^{D-N}\times [-1,1]^N$ can never be diffeomorphisms. It suffers from discontinuity when $q$ contains zero-coordinate like $(1, 0, 0, 0)$ the identity or $(0, 0, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$.

The exponential map flows is defined as:

$$
f(x)=\exp_x\nabla\phi(x)=x\cos\vert \nabla\phi(x)\vert+\frac{\nabla\phi(x)}{\vert\nabla\phi(x)\vert}\sin\vert\nabla\phi(x)\vert,
$$

where $\nabla\phi(x)$ is the gradient to $\phi(x)$ at $x$,

$$
\phi(x) = \sum_i\frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}\exp(\beta_i(x^T \mu_i-1))
$$

$$
\nabla\phi(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\exp(\beta_i(x^T \mu_i-1)) \mu_i
$$

The exponential map flows can't satisfy the requirement of $f(q) = -f(-q)$ as $\nabla\phi(x) \neq -\nabla\phi(-x)$.

Therefore, it's non-trivial to apply this method to SO(3) using the quaternion representation. We 're wondering how to construct such flows based on this method and how to use symmetry enforcement.

[1] Rezende et al.: Normalizing Flows on Tori and Spheres, ICML 2020

content.title: Author Response(1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback and comments on our writing. We're proofreading our paper and it'll be updated soon. Here are some responses to the comments.

> “To further increase the expressivity of the M ̈obius transformation, Rezende et al. (2020) leveraged linear combination” – I’m unsure of the novelty of the paper, do both the mobius transformation and linear combination transformation appear in Rezende et al. 2020? Is it that the work is an application of NF for general riemannian manifolds, with the novelty primarily in the identification and resolution of issues specific to SO(3)?

The mobius transformation is presented in Rezende et al. (2020) to construct normalizing flows on Tori, however, our method is very different from theirs, in our mobius coupling design and quaternion affine transformation.

The mobius coupling interprets SO(3) as three orthonormal 3-vectors, pick one vector to predict parameters orthogonal to the vector, and applies the mobius transformation to get a new vector orthogonal to the unchanged vector. These two vectors fully determine the third orthonormal vector and give a new SO(3). Our coupling layers fully utilize the topology of SO(3) rotation matrix and is very intuitive.

The **coupling layer** design can also be interpreted more elegantly as a bundle isomorphism. It uses the fiber bundle with projection $\pi:SO(3)\rightarrow SO(2)$ and fiber $S^1 = SO(2)$ . Choosing the conditioning dimension $i=1,2,3$  defines one such projection, for each base space point $c_1$ , there is a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(c_1) \rightarrow \pi^{-1}(c_1)$ over its fiber, which together form a base-space preserving bundle isomorphism. Our mobius coupling layers may help generalization to other fiber bundles.

Rezende et al. (2020) take the weighted sum of the angles in combining mobius transformation, however, we discover this simple treatment can suffer from discontinuity, and use a $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ trick to **solve the singularity**. It should be noted that this **linear combination is different from our proposed quaternion affine transformation**. The linear combination is implemented to increase the expressivity of mobius transformation, and the quaternion affine transformation is another module that is applied to the quaternion representation.

The linear combination of mobius transformation is implemented as follows: the network predicted K different  $\omega$ coordinate(parameters for a mobius transformation) and its corresponding weights, and angles between the transformed points with its original one are weighted to compute the output point. Assume the weights are 0.5 and 0.5 for 2 combined transformations, angles are 30$^\circ$ and $50^\circ$ , and the output angle will be 40$^\circ$, therefore the output vector can be calculated. However, as angles are constrained to $[-\pi, \pi]$, some slight change around $\pi$ will cause discontinuity in the output. Assume one angle is 30 $^\circ$, and the other is $-178^\circ$, [0.5, 0.5] weights give a combined angle $-74^\circ$; however, when the other is $-182^\circ$, or $178^\circ$, which is very close to $-178^\circ$, [0.5, 0.5] weights give a combined angle $104^\circ$. The slight change of angles gives a great change in combined output. However, we solve such a problem by restricting $\omega$ within a $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ sphere, therefore angles between the transformed points with its original one will be constrained to $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ and won't cause singularity mentioned below.

The quaternion affine transformation is defined as:

$$
g(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{W\mathbf{q}}{\vert W\mathbf{q}\vert}
$$

where W is a 4$\times$ 4 invertible matrix and $\mathbf{q}$ the quaternion representation of a rotation. The affine transformation is really novel and elegant. It can perform 2 functions, a rotation operation and a scaling operation at the same time. By SVD decomposition, W can be decomposed into U, S, V, whereas U and V serve as global rotations ( can be interpreted as a shift for elements in SO(3)) and S serves as a scaling term. With a resemblance to affine transformation in Euclidean space $f=ax+b$, we call it quaternion affine transformation. The rotation operation not only makes it easier to learn a global rotation but also serves as a generalization of permutation in our mobius coupling layers. The scaling operation can quickly concentrate distributions and improve performance.

content.title: Author Response(2/2)
content.comment:
> In the results the authors note that Falorsi et al. fails to fit the sharp distribution around the identity because of a singularity. Is this a consequence of their choice of parameterization? If so, I think it would help the reader to know what parameterization they use.

To be specific, the method of Faloris et al. 2019 suffers from discontinuity on the pi-sphere due to the axis-angle representation.  And it fails whenever tries to fit a peak distribution around any point in SO(3). In our implementation, we discover that the probability density is unnormalized and it does not appear to be a constant, thus it’s needy to calculate the normalizing constant. To complete the calculation, we need to sample points in the whole axis-angle space and compute their possibilities. For very peak distribution, the flow learned to map nearly all points in the pi-sphere of the latent space to points around the peak, and inversely, points away from the peak are corresponding to points near the pi-sphere of the latent space, as it used a *tanh* to constrain points in pi-sphere. The unconstrained vectors in the Euclidean space before *tanh* are so large that it becomes NAN, therefore their probabilities can’t be calculated. As it fails to compute the normalizing constant, the log-likelihood is impossible to compute.

Example: In fitting distributions of synthetic data, the log normalizing constant is calculated to be

| iteration | 0    | 250   | 500   | 750   | 1000  | 1500   | 2000  |
| --------- | ---- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ------ | ----- |
| cube-like | 1.22 | -2.58 | -2.30 | -2.00 | -2.29 | -0.572 | -2.38 |
| cone-like | 1.24 | -0.21 | -0.91 | -1.16 | -0.41 | 0.006  | -0.58 |

The sample size is set to 100,000,000 each, and it's clear that the normalizing constant is not preserved. If we neglect all NAN encountered in calculating the distribution of samples in peak distribution fitting, the log normalizing constant will be -9, which we believe is not plausible.

> “In practice, we represent 4 × 4 invertible matrix by a unconstrained 4 × 4 matrix...” Do the authors find that the matrices are generally well conditioned? Have the authors experimented with other approaches?

Though there is some possibility of singularity for an unconstrained parameterization, it is invertible almost everywhere. During our implementation, it’s very safe and numerically stable.

We also implemented an unconstrained parametrization: P * L * (U +  *diag* (S)) used in Glow and found no noticeable difference in density fitting of unconditioned data. So we believe the unconstrained 4$\times$ 4 matrix is enough for parameterization for our case.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a discrete normalizing flow for the SO(3) manifold via two coupling layers:
- A Möbius-like transformation:  interpret SO(3) as three orthonormal 3-vectors $(c_1, c_2, c_3)$. pick i=1,2,3, j $\neq$ i, use a neural network given $c_i$ to predict a $w \in \mathbb R^3$ orthogonal to $c_i$. Then apply the Möbius transformation for $c_j$ along $w$ to get new vector $c'_j$ orthogonal to $c_i$. These two vectors fully define the third orthonormal vectors, giving a new SO(3) matrix.
- Interpret SO(3) as the 3d real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^3$, then act with an invertible linear transformation of the ambient space $\mathbb R^4$ on $\mathbb{RP}^3$.

These two layers are interleaved to form a normalizing flow. The method is evaluated against several prior works and performs favourably on image density modelling datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The method is elegant.
- The method is stable and performs well.
- The evaluation against prior works is thorough.
- As stated below, the Mobius transformation could be used as a blueprint to design flows on other fiber bundles.

Weakness:
- The claim that the proposed flows "can be arbitrarily flexible" should be nuanced unless the authors can prove their flow is universally expressive.
- I'm not quite sure about the statement that the method of Falorsi et al. 2019 inherently suffers from poles around the identity. The exponential map should be well behaved around the identity, at least in theory. In implementation, some removable poles might occur in the used equations though. Lacking the exponential map, I can still imagine the proposed method to be more stable overall than the method in Falorsi 2019.
- I'm not very convinced about the statement that the invertible matrix can be safely parametrized to be unconstrained, as the probability of singularity is "near-zero". The parameter isn't sampled from a uniform distribution, but learned and depending on the loss function, might be encouraged to become singular.

Additional suggestion:
- It appears like the Möbius transform can be elegantly interpreted as a bundle isomorphism. It uses the fiber bundle with projection $\pi: SO(3) \to S^2$ and fiber $S^1=SO(2)$. Choosing the conditioning dimension $i=1,2,3$ defines one such projection, for each base space point $c_1$, there is a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(c_1) \to \pi^{-1}(c_1)$ over its fiber, which together form a base-space preserving bundle isomorphism. Adding this interpretation to the paper might encourage generalization to other fiber bundles.
- Why is the affine transform not just called a linear transformation, as there is no shift?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is very clear and pleasant to read. The illustrations are very helpful.

Quality: the theoretical and empirical claims are mostly well-supported.

Novelty: as far as I know, the method is the first practical and simple SO(3) flow.

Reproducibility: sufficient.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is simple and performs well on SO(3) density modelling, which has very useful applications in e.g. robotics and natural sciences. Strong paper, good contribution to conference.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes to estimate the density function over SO(3) using normalizing flows. 
Key to constructing normalizing flow networks are the invertible coupling and affine layers
and the computation of the Jacobian of each layer needed for the transformation of the density. The coupling layer in this paper uses a Moebius transform while the affine layer switches to a quaternion representation and computes a 1x1 convolution. Evaluation is on orientation samples from human pose data and on SYMSOL.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The authors are aware of the continuity issue of SO(3) representations and make the choice to represent SO(3) with a 9D representation. 
+ The Moebius coupling layer is very carefully designed: the second column c2 of a rotation matrix transforms via a Moebius transform conditioned on the first column c1. Since c3=c1xc2 this c2 and c3 are transformed together conditioned on c1.
+ The authors explained well the scaling and normalization part of the affine layer. 
+ The authors evaluate on SYMSOL I and II and outperform the creators of the datasets (IPDF) as well as three other state-of-the-art orientation density estimators.

The weaknesses of the paper concern the affine layer and the experimental evaluation.

-: Please explain why we have to take the weighted sum of the angles in combining multiple layers. This came out of the blue, given that the authors are aware of the underlying discontinuities. There are several ways to combine rotations in the SO(3) interpolation literature; see also Semidefinite descriptions of the convex hull of rotation matrices by Saunderson et al.

-: Authors do not motivate why they switched to quaternions for the "1x1 convolution" layer. 
"We choose to implement this rotation operation in quaternion space rather than directly in SO(3), because it is naturally covered by quaternion affine transformation, and also, parametrizing a 3 × 3 rotation matrix is harder than a 4 × 4 invertible matrix."
Authors should clarify what they mean. 
The first argument does not hold, they could use the first two columns of the rotation matrix multiplied by a 6x6 linear matrix. 

-: "In practice, we represent 4 × 4 invertible matrix by an unconstrained 4 × 4 matrix as the probability for a non-invertible matrix is near-zero."
If this were true, then the authors of Glow and other papers would not have constructed the layers in a way that they are invertible deterministically and not in probability. 
Why not use the Perm*(L*(U+diag(s))) ?

-: The 1x1 convolution in Glow is applied on the channels, which here are the representation of the rotation matrix. However, SO(3) representation theory gives several ways how to build a linear operation on any vector space so that this operation would be isomorphic to SO(3). 

-: The experimental evaluation is only on SYMSOL and orientation samples from UP-3D, H3.6M etc. However, the implicit pdf paper (Murphy et al. ) has very realistic examples where their normalizing flow is conditioned on real examples of object and human kinematic pose. Such real examples can show why one should use normalized flow for orientation densities and not implicit pdf's.

-: In the implementation, authors must clarify whether the uniform distribution is over R^9 or over rotation matrices. content.title: Author Response(1/2)
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedback! The following are our responses.

> Please explain why we have to take the weighted sum of the angles in combining multiple layers. This came out of the blue, given that the authors are aware of the underlying discontinuities. There are several ways to combine rotations in the SO(3) interpolation literature; see also Semidefinite descriptions of the convex hull of rotation matrices by Saunderson et al.

Though weighted sum of the angles in combining multiple layers can suffer from discontinuities, our trick of constraining $\omega$ within $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ can alleviate the problem. By stacking multiple layers, our flows can be very flexible and express variable distributions.

> Authors do not motivate why they switched to quaternions for the "1x1 convolution" layer. "We choose to implement this rotation operation in quaternion space rather than directly in SO(3), because it is naturally covered by quaternion affine transformation, and also, parametrizing a 3 × 3 rotation matrix is harder than a 4 × 4 invertible matrix." Authors should clarify what they mean. The first argument does not hold, they could use the first two columns of the rotation matrix multiplied by a 6x6 linear matrix.

The motivation is that the topology of quaternions is simpler than rotation matrix, and has less degree of freedom. So the affine transformation will have fewer parameters and is easier.  If we perform a transformation on the first two columns of the rotation matrix, due to the topology of two columns (they are in the Stiefel manifold), the transformed 6 vectors should be projected to the Stiefel manifold (maybe by Schmidt orthogonalization), and the projection may not be bijective. Also, we can give some examples:

Assume that the rotation matrix before transformation is:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\\0&1&0\\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
$$

That the 6-D vector is :

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\\0\\\0\\\0\\\1\\\0\end{pmatrix}
$$

The $6\times6$  invertible linear matrix is in the form:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1&\times&\times\\\0&\times&\times\\\0&\times&\times\\\ & & & \times&1&\times\\\ & & & \times&0&\times\\\ & & & \times&0&\times\end{pmatrix}
$$

The transformed vector will be,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\\0\\\0\\\0\\\0\\\0\end{pmatrix}
$$

which can not be projected to the first two columns of the rotation matrix. So there'll be more constraints on the $6\times 6$ linear matrix, and is much more difficult to implement.

> "In practice, we represent 4 × 4 invertible matrix by an unconstrained 4 × 4 matrix as the probability for a non-invertible matrix is near-zero." If this were true, then the authors of Glow and other papers would not have constructed the layers in a way that they are invertible deterministically and not in probability. Why not use the Perm*(L*(U+diag(s))) ?

Though there is some possibility of singularity, the unconstrained parametrization of matrix is invertible almost everywhere, and during our implementation, it’s safe.

We also implemented an unconstrained parametrization: P * L * (U +  *diag* (S)) used in Glow, and found no noticeable difference at least in density fitting of unconditioned data. Detailed results will be updated soon.

> *The 1x1 convolution in Glow is applied on the channels, which here are the representation of the rotation matrix. However, SO(3) representation theory gives several ways how to build a linear operation on any vector space so that this operation would be isomorphic to SO(3).*

We 're wondering what's the "several ways" to build a linear operation, could you please give some examples? The common representations of SO(3) are rotation matrix, quaternion, axis-angle, and Euler angles. The euler angles is discontinuous at the origin, and axis-angle is discontinuous on the pi-sphere. As stated before, it's more difficult to construct linear operation on rotation matrix, as there's a more strick requirement for the topology of rotation matrix. So it's more plausible to construct such operations on quaternion.

> The experimental evaluation is only on SYMSOL and orientation samples from UP-3D, H3.6M etc. However, the implicit pdf paper (Murphy et al. ) has very realistic examples where their normalizing flow is conditioned on real examples of object and human kinematic pose. Such real examples can show why one should use normalized flow for orientation densities and not implicit pdf's.

More experimental evaluations will be updated soon. However, implicit pdf paper is only conditioned on real examples of objects, not on human kinematic pose.

content.title: Concerning Rotation Combinations
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, you mentioned that "There are several ways to combine rotations in the SO(3) interpolation literature; see also Semidefinite descriptions of the convex hull of rotation matrices by Saunderson et al."

Semidefinite descriptions of the convex hull of rotation matrices studied the convex hull of SO(n) and showed that the convex hull of SO(n) is doubly spectrahedral, that it and its polar have a description as the intersection of a cone of positive semidefinite matrices with an affine subspace. In their work, the mathematic structure of convex hull of SO(n) is presented, however, how to apply rotation combination in this way is still not studied and not clear. As for other methods to combine rotations, could you please give some other hints and suggestions?

As our Mobius coupling layer pick one column unchanged as a condition  and transform the other column to get a new vector that is orthogonal to the condition column, the transformation only has 1 Degree of Freedom which we denote by $\theta$. So in fact we're combining 1 Degree of Freedom rotations. Therefore the weighted sum of angles is a natural choice. There're other methods like vector combinations and then normalizing to a unit vector, which, we argue can still have a singularity.

Take the equal combination of antipolar points for example. Assume the two points are $\mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{-c}$, and the combined point will be zero. If $-\mathbf{c}$ slightly changes to $(\mathbf{-c}+\Delta)$ ($\mathbf{\Delta}$ is an infinitesimal vector), the combined point will be $\mathbf{\Delta}/\vert \Delta\vert$. If $-c$ slightly changed to $(\mathbf{-c-\Delta})$, the combined point will be $-\mathbf{\Delta}/\vert \Delta\vert$. A slight change in vectors will cause a great change in combined points. Therefore we still need the $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ trick presented in our paper to constrain points on one inferior arc.
